exercises.objective: Derive that potential-based reward shaping's optimal value function is the original value function shifted by the potential.
exercises.prompt: Given $V^*$ solves RL-01's Bellman optimality equation for reward $R$, verify by direct substitution that $V'(s):=V^*(s)-\Phi(s)$ solves the Bellman optimality equation for the shaped reward $R'(s,a,s')=R(s,a,s')+\gamma\Phi(s')-\Phi(s)$.
hints: Write the shaped Bellman equation: $V'(s)=\max_a\mathbb{E}_{s'}\{R(s,a,s')+\gamma\Phi(s')-\Phi(s)+\gamma V'(s')\}$. Since $-\Phi(s)$ doesn't depend on $a$ or $s'$, factor it out: $V'(s)=-\Phi(s)+\max_a\mathbb{E}_{s'}\{R(s,a,s')+\gamma[\Phi(s')+V'(s')]\}$.
Substitute the guess $V'(s')=V^*(s')-\Phi(s')$ into the bracket: $\Phi(s')+V'(s')=\Phi(s')+V^*(s')-\Phi(s')=V^*(s')$.

So $V'(s)=-\Phi(s)+\max_a\mathbb{E}_{s'}\{R(s,a,s')+\gamma V^*(s')\}=-\Phi(s)+V^*(s)$, exactly the guess: $V'(s)=V^*(s)-\Phi(s)$ is confirmed to be a consistent fixed point. Since $\Phi(s)$ doesn't depend on $a$, the $\operatorname*{argmax}_a$ (the optimal policy) is completely unchanged. (Independently verified numerically on a random small MDP while authoring this module.)

exercises.objective: Explain why on-policy data requirements are a genuine bottleneck for training deep RL on physical robots.
exercises.prompt: Explain why needing (near-)on-policy data is a much bigger practical problem for a physical robot than for a simulated one.
hints: In simulation, generating a fresh rollout under the current policy costs only compute time, which is cheap and fully parallelizable.

On a physical robot, generating a fresh rollout requires real wall-clock time, physical wear, potential safety risk, and often human supervision, none of which parallelize or speed up the way simulated compute does.

So an algorithm needing frequently-refreshed on-policy data (rather than being able to reuse a large stored buffer of older, off-policy data) imposes a real-world sample-collection cost that dominates practical training time on hardware, exactly why so much robot RL happens in simulation first (RLEARN-04).

exercises.objective: Explain why temporally-correlated exploration noise gives better state coverage than naive per-step noise.
exercises.prompt: Explain why pink noise or an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process gives better exploration coverage than i.i.d. per-step (Brownian-like) random noise, for the same number of environment steps.
hints: I.i.d. per-step noise has zero correlation between consecutive actions, so its effects on the system tend to average out (a push one way is nearly as likely to be undone by a push the other way the very next step), producing lots of small, self-cancelling jitter rather than genuine excursions to new states.
Temporally-correlated noise (pink noise, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) instead tends to push in a similar direction over several consecutive steps before reversing, producing coherent, sustained excursions.

This directly parallels RLEARN-01's 'good data' principle (system identification needs frequency coverage, not just any input): sustained, structured excursions actually explore new parts of state space per unit of real-robot time, where uncorrelated jitter mostly cancels itself out and covers less ground.
